extraction_text: The speaker uses various metaphors to illustrate principles of governance and wisdom.

extraction_text: The speaker concludes with observations on human behavior and satisfaction.

attributes.relationships: General advice applicable to all, especially rulers.

extraction_text: The text warns that a king who cannot control his own senses will bring chaos to his kingdom and be destroyed by his own actions.

attributes.relationships: Advice for rulers on governance and self-mastery.

attributes.relationships: General moral contrast between good and evil conduct.
attributes.supernatural_elements: References to karmic consequences: '谩骂者获得罪恶，宽容者获得解脱' (The slanderer acquires sin, the tolerant attains liberation).

extraction_text: Vidura advises Dhritarashtra about the importance of righteous speech and justice over ritualistic practices.

attributes.relationships: Dhritarashtra is the king seeking advice; Vidura is his wise counselor and half-brother.
attributes.key_points: Vidura emphasizes that mercy and justice toward all beings are superior to ritual bathing at holy places. He urges Dhritarashtra to be just to his sons (the Kauravas) to gain honor in this life and heaven after death.

extraction_text: Vidura recounts an ancient dialogue between Keshini, Virochana, and Shukra (also known as Ushanas or Kavya) about the superiority of Brahmins versus Daityas (demons).

attributes.relationships: Keshini is a woman questioning Virochana; Virochana is a Daitya prince, son of Prahlada; Shukra is a sage and preceptor of the Daityas.
attributes.key_points: Keshini asks whether Brahmins or Daityas are superior and whom Shukra avoids sitting with. Virochana claims Daityas are superior as descendants of Prahlada. Keshini arranges a meeting between Virochana and Shukra to witness their interaction.

extraction_text: Shukra refuses to sit with Virochana on an equal seat, leading to a confrontation about status and worthiness.

attributes.relationships: Shukra is a Brahmin sage; Virochana is a Daitya prince. Shukra implicitly asserts Brahmin superiority by refusing equal seating.
attributes.key_points: Shukra accepts a golden chair from Virochana but states he will not sit with him. Virochana retorts that Shukra is unworthy of the same chair and should sit on a board, grass, or mat instead.

extraction_text: Virocana and Sukesa argue about their fathers' status and make a wager.
Virocana suggests wagering gold, cattle, horses, and Asura wealth to consult learned people.
Sukesa rejects material wager and proposes wagering their lives instead.
Virocana questions where to go with life wager since he never stands before gods or mortals.
Sukesa suggests going to Virocana's father Prahlada with the life wager.

attributes.reason: Prahlada won't lie even for his son

extraction_text: Prahlada observes Virocana and Sukesa approaching together and questions their unusual companionship.

extraction_text: Prahlada offers water, honey food, and a white bull to Sukesa as hospitality.

attributes.action: Philosophical inquiry about truth and arbitration

extraction_text: Sukesa describes the suffering of false arbitrators using metaphors and explains consequences of lying for different things.

extraction_text: A wise person learns wisdom from the wise, gains righteousness and benefits through wisdom, and enjoys happiness.

Complete work during the day and rest peacefully at night; complete work in eight months and rest during the rainy season; complete work in youth and rest in old age; complete work in life and enjoy benefits after death.
People praise digested food, a wife past her youth, a hero after battle, and an ascetic who has reached success.
Using ill-gotten wealth to fill one hole only creates another hole.
Teachers control those with souls, kings control evil-souled people, and Yama (son of Vivasvat) controls secret evildoers.

supernatural_elements: Yama as divine controller of death

extraction_text: The origins of sages, rivers, noble families, and women's misdeeds are unknowable.
Generous donors who like to give to Brahmins, righteous people who treat relatives well, and Kshatriyas who enjoy heaven will permanently rule the earth.
Three types of people obtain the earth with golden flowers: warriors, scholars, and those who know service.
Intellectual action is best, arm strength is medium, leg strength is next, and brute strength is worst.
Dhritarashtra (implied king) gives power to foolish Duryodhana, Shakuni, Duhshasana, and Karna, and cannot expect prosperity.
The Pandavas possess all virtues, treat Dhritarashtra as a father, and he should treat them as sons.
This concludes Chapter 35 of the Udyoga Parva in the Mahabharata.
